title: Solar CRM Software: 7 Tools Compared for Solar Companies
html:
Solar CRM software should track every lead from first call to permit, and a free tool is enough to start. Pick one system for leads, one for proposals and one for follow-up, then link them to your lead generation channels. Published prices in this guide run from $0 to $297 a month, and solar-specific tools often hide pricing behind a sales call.

Solar CRM software has to do three jobs: catch the lead, move it through the sale and keep the project on track after the contract. Most solar companies pick a tool for one job and then patch the rest with spreadsheets and text messages. This guide sorts seven tools by the job each one does, with the price each vendor publishes and one real limit for each.

A solar sale is long. A homeowner compares quotes, asks about financing, waits on permits and expects updates the whole way. That means a lead that goes quiet for a week is often a lead lost.

Which solar CRM software is built for solar sales?

OpenSolar and Enerflo are the two solar-specific platforms in this guide. Both cover more of the sale than a general CRM, but they work in different ways.

The choice comes down to who owns the lead record. OpenSolar bundles a CRM with design and proposals, so a small crew can run on one tool. Enerflo describes itself as a layer that works with the tools you already use, so you still need somewhere to store the lead.

Whichever you pick, the lead has to arrive first. Rankings from solar SEO and paid search from solar Google Ads are the two sources that fill a pipeline most predictably.

Which general CRM works for a small solar company?

HubSpot, monday CRM and Zoho CRM suit a solar company that wants one place for contacts, deals and tasks without paying for design software. All three publish a free or entry plan.

None of these three stores a roof layout or a financing offer. You would pair them with a design and proposal tool. That split is fine if you keep one rule: the CRM is the only place a lead status is edited.

The CRM that wins is the one your sales reps update the same day, not the one with the longest feature list.

Which tools automate follow-up with solar leads?

GoHighLevel and Jobber automate different parts of the follow-up. GoHighLevel focuses on texts, emails and campaigns, while Jobber focuses on quotes and scheduled visits.

Automation only helps when the message is worth sending. A first text that arrives within minutes, a reminder before the site visit and a check-in after the proposal cover most of the gap.

What stages should a solar CRM pipeline have?

A solar CRM pipeline needs six to eight stages that match how a real sale moves, from new lead to installed system. Fewer stages hide where deals stall. More stages make reps skip the updates.

StageWhat to logRule of thumb
New leadSource, phone, address, roof typeReply the same day, by text first
ContactedDate of first live conversationThree attempts before you pause a lead
Site visit bookedDate, rep, utility bill receivedSend a reminder the day before
Proposal sentDate, system size, financing optionFollow up two days later
Contract signedDate, deposit, lenderHand off to project tracking
Permit and installPermit status, install dateMessage the homeowner at each change
InstalledDate, review request sentAsk for a review within a week

Name each stage after something a rep can verify. "Proposal sent" is a fact. "Warm" is an opinion. Facts keep your reports honest, and they make it easy to see whether the weak step is your lead source or your sales follow-up.

How do you set up a solar CRM in the first week?

Set up a solar CRM in five steps and finish before you add any automation. A messy start gets automated at scale.

  1. Load open leads. Import the leads you are still working, and archive the rest so they do not clutter the board.
  2. Build the stages. Use the table above, and delete any stage nobody will update.
  3. Tag the source. Give each lead a source such as website, map listing, paid search or referral.
  4. Write three messages. Draft a first reply, a visit reminder and a proposal check-in in plain language.
  5. Name one owner. One person reviews stale leads every Monday.

The Monday review matters more than the tool. Sort by days since last contact and call the oldest. Most CRMs, including every tool above, can produce that view in a minute.

What should feed a solar CRM besides your own calls?

A solar CRM fills from three sources: your website, your Google listing and paid search. If those are weak, the best software in the world manages an empty list.

Other trades face the same wiring problem. The remodeling CRM automation cost guide gives the budget view.

What mistakes do solar companies make with CRM software?

The most common mistake is buying software to fix a lead problem. A CRM manages leads you already have, so an empty pipeline needs marketing first. Five other mistakes show up again and again.

  • Too many fields: a form with twenty required fields makes reps skip it. Require five and make the rest optional.
  • No source tag: without it you cannot tell whether search, ads or referrals produce signed installs.
  • Two systems of record: if proposals live in one tool and lead notes in another, pick which one owns the status.
  • Automation before process: a bad follow-up sequence sent to every lead damages trust faster than silence.
  • No export plan: keep a monthly export of your leads so a pricing change never traps your data.

Each of these is cheap to fix before launch and expensive to fix after a year of messy data. Spend one afternoon on the setup steps above and you avoid most of them.

How do you choose solar CRM software?

Choose solar CRM software with a three-check filter: fit, cost and setup effort. Run every tool through all three before you pay.

Fit: does it hold the lead, the proposal and the permit stage, or do you need a second tool for each?

Cost: add the plan price, extra seats, texting fees and any add-on, then compare the total against the gross profit on one average install.

Setup effort: can one person load your open leads and build three follow-up messages in a weekend?

A two-person crew that sells a few systems a month can run on HubSpot's free plan for leads and OpenSolar for design and proposals. A larger sales team with several reps and a financing-heavy offer is a better fit for Enerflo plus a CRM that reports on rep activity.

Here is a cost example using standard published prices. A free HubSpot plan plus OpenSolar costs $0 in plan fees. Three HubSpot Starter seats at the standard $20 each cost $60 a month. GoHighLevel Starter is $97 a month before usage fees. Add texting and any add-on before you compare.

Before you sign, ask each vendor three questions. What does texting cost per message? Who answers support when a rep cannot find a proposal? A vendor that dodges the first question is a vendor you may not be able to leave.

What is the best CRM for a solar company?

There is no single best choice, because it depends on team size and sales process. A small crew can start with a free CRM such as HubSpot and add OpenSolar for design and proposals. Larger teams that sell financing should check Enerflo, which does not publish pricing.

How much does solar CRM software cost?

Published prices in this guide run from free to $297 a month. HubSpot and OpenSolar describe free options, monday CRM Basic is $12 per seat, and GoHighLevel starts at $97. Texting fees, extra seats and add-ons cost more, and Enerflo does not publish pricing.

Is there free CRM software for solar installers?

Yes. HubSpot's free plan covers up to 2 users and 1,000 contacts, and Zoho CRM's free edition covers up to 3 users. OpenSolar describes its design and project software as free. Free plans limit automation, so expect to upgrade when follow-up volume grows.

Do solar companies need a CRM and proposal software?

Most do, because a general CRM does not design systems or build financing offers. Solar-specific tools such as OpenSolar and Enerflo cover proposals. A CRM still holds the lead history, so many companies run both and keep one system as the source of truth.

What should a solar CRM track?

Track the lead source, the first contact time, the site visit, the proposal date and the contract date. Add the permit stage if your tool allows it. These fields show where leads stall and which marketing channel actually produces signed installs.

Can CRM automation replace a solar sales rep?

No. Automation sends the first text, reminders and check-ins, but a rep still has to explain savings, financing and timelines. Use automation to make sure no lead waits, and keep a person on every conversation that reaches the proposal stage.

Where do solar leads for a CRM come from?

Most come from search rankings, paid search ads, map listings and referrals. The CRM only stores and routes them. Connect your website forms and call tracking to the CRM so each lead carries a source tag you can report on later.
